chapter_theme: The first verses of the Naattu sarukkam describe the land as a place where hills, farms, pastures and shore each give their own sounds and flowers: a country of festival, bees and honey, whose women's beauty and perfumes reach even ascetics.

7.reading: The country is a city set round with a jewelled hill, rivalling the Vidyadhara world in festival, and its wealth is said never to sleep; the name Surumai ends the verse.
7.nuance: The last line's wealth-that-sleeps and the name சுரமை are hard to construe after the edition's repair of line 4.

8.reading: Lotus beds, shoals of red carp and the women's faces and eyes are set side by side, so the land's waters and its women share one beauty.

9.reading: Women's swan-like walk and soft speech make the cool fields ring, and the villages ring in turn with the anklets on their small feet.

10.reading: Bees and parrots fill the groves while the houses are full of the speech and lutes of women.
10.nuance: Line 2 has a repaired letter; the sense is plain.

11.reading: Scented water-flowers and women's perfumes are so heavy that they weaken even the ascetics who stand in good austerity.
11.nuance: The poet lets the land's sweetness reach the austere: a quiet admission that the senses test the renouncer, in a work whose later sarukkams praise renunciation.

12.reading: Mountain, forest, farmland and shore, the four regions, are all found together in this one land.
12.nuance: Line 2 reads திணையுந தேரல்சேர் in the edition (a likely misprint) and line 4 ends oddly; the four-region claim is clear.

13.reading: Festival drums, falling streams and the roar of elephants together fill the air on one side of the land.

14.reading: On one side of the land the cowherds' drums, their sweet konrai-flutes and their shouting fill the pastures.

15.reading: On another side the sound of festival drums, flocks of birds and the plough-song of the fields is joined.

16.reading: On the coast the music of the fishers, the children's play, the shore's noise and the surge of waves are all heard.

17.reading: Kandal, blue lilies and vengai flower on the hills, and the honey of the high slopes runs thick like ghee.

18.reading: Konrai, kurundu, kotal and the jasmine bowers fill the village commons with scent and drip honey.

19.reading: The seashore's lilies, red lotus beds and the bees on them pour out honey that flows everywhere on one side of the land.

20.reading: The seaside groves, with their screwpine, blue lilies and parrots, look like a wishing-tree forest.

21.reading: On the high hills, peacocks dance whenever the great clouds roar over the peaks.

links.note: The verse praises the land by festival and wealth only; Kural 738 lists freedom from disease, protection and yield as a land's ornaments.
links.teaches: The epic shows a land's greatness by its splendour alone, so the reader sees what the Kural's list adds that this praise leaves out.

gains.a: A test of what a land's wealth should rest on, which a bare picture of splendour lacks.
gains.b: A concrete land to which the five ornaments can be held up, where the couplet only names them.

links.note: Women's perfumes weaken even ascetics here; the Thiruppugazh poet confesses his own ruin from craving women.
links.teaches: The scenic verse already carries the temptation that the poet of the Thiruppugazh later tells in the first person.

gains.a: A named cost of the pleasure it lightly sketches, which the verse itself does not state.
gains.b: An earlier poetic case in which the same allure reaches ascetics, not only a self-confessed sinner.

links.note: Both set the regions of the Tamil land together in one country: the four regions mingled here, the tunes and creatures of each region exchanged there.
links.teaches: Both poems prove a country's wholeness by letting the four regions share each other's things, but the epic only lists them while the Pattupattu ties the mingling to the king's just rule.

gains.a: A political reason for the blend, the king's one umbrella, which the epic's list leaves unsaid.
gains.b: A plain statement that the regions simply lie together, without the court's praise.

links.note: Both set the cowherds' flute in the evening pastures: a sign of plenty here, a torment to the waiting wife there.
links.teaches: The same flute is joy in the public landscape and pain in a private heart, so the reader sees how the sound takes its meaning from who hears it.

gains.a: A listener inside the scene, which the epic's description does not give.
gains.b: A public, cheerful reading of the flute against which her pain stands out.

links.note: Peacocks dance to the clouds' roar here, and in Akananuru 82 the hill is a stage where the peacock is the dancer.
links.teaches: Both make the hill a stage on which weather and creatures perform together, but the Akananuru names the full orchestra while the epic gives only clouds and peacocks.

gains.a: A fuller account of how the hill's sounds become music, which it only hints at.
gains.b: The same scene shown as ordinary prosperity, free of a lover's longing.

source_issues: Verse 7 line 4: TSCII leftover letters repaired (நிதியது); the reading of the last line stays doubtful.
Verses 10: one repaired letter in line 2.
Verse 12 line 2 reads திணையுந தேரல்சேர் and line 4 ends oddly, probably misprints.
